title: Free Indirect Discourse
text:
Free indirect discourse is a narrative technique that blends a character's thoughts with the narrator's voice. In the novels of Jane Austen, this technique allows the reader to witness a character's inner judgments without the intrusion of quotation marks. The effect is often ironic, since the narrator's tone can gently expose the gap between what a character believes and what is actually true. Readers must therefore remain alert to subtle shifts in perspective.

Writers who employ this technique must balance intimacy with distance. Too much access to a character's mind can make the narration feel claustrophobic, while too little can leave the reader disengaged. Austen mastered this balance by allowing her heroines' reflections to color the prose while retaining a wry, detached authority. As a result, the reader feels both sympathy and skepticism toward the protagonist.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what does free indirect discourse combine?
options: A character's thoughts with the narrator's voice
Dialogue with a summary of events
Two different narrators in one chapter
A letter with a diary entry

questions.text: What does the second paragraph say may happen when a writer gives too little access to a character's mind?
What can be inferred about the narrator's tone in Austen's novels?
options: It is always openly critical of the heroines
It can quietly expose the gap between belief and reality
It is completely neutral and objective
It shifts entirely to the dialogue of other characters

questions.text: Why does the reader feel both sympathy and skepticism toward the protagonist?
options: Because the reader sees her thoughts while the narrator keeps a detached authority
Because the narrator never reveals her thoughts
Because the story is told in the first person
Because the heroine speaks only in dialogue

paragraph_translations: El discurso indirecto libre es una técnica narrativa que combina los pensamientos de un personaje con la voz del narrador. En las novelas de Jane Austen, esta técnica permite al lector presenciar los juicios internos de un personaje sin la intrusión de las comillas. El efecto suele ser irónico, ya que el tono del narrador puede exponer con suavidad la distancia entre lo que el personaje cree y lo que es realmente cierto. Por ello, el lector debe mantenerse atento a los cambios sutiles de perspectiva.

Los escritores que emplean esta técnica deben equilibrar la cercanía y la distancia. Un acceso excesivo a la mente de un personaje puede hacer que la narración resulte claustrofóbica, mientras que un acceso insuficiente puede dejar al lector desconectado. Austen dominó este equilibrio al permitir que las reflexiones de sus heroínas tiñeran la prosa, conservando a la vez una autoridad irónica y distante. Como resultado, el lector siente tanto simpatía como escepticismo hacia la protagonista.
